en.title: Scientists and inventors
en.summary: Famous scientists and inventors from English-speaking countries, with the grammar of discovery.

sections.title: About this lesson
paragraphs: People from the United Kingdom, Ireland, the United States and other English-speaking countries have given the world many discoveries. In this lesson you will meet eight of them. You will also learn how English describes discoveries: with the passive, with purpose clauses, and with the word endings that name people and inventions.

sections.title: In context
paragraphs:
| Person | Known for | When |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Isaac Newton, England | the laws of motion and the law of gravity | published in 1687 |
| Charles Darwin, England | the theory of evolution by natural selection | On the Origin of Species, 1859 |
| Ada Lovelace, England | notes on Babbage's machine that include what is often called the first computer program | 1843 |
| Alexander Graham Bell, born in Scotland | the telephone | patent in the United States, 1876 |
| Orville and Wilbur Wright, the United States | the first powered aeroplane flight | 1903 |
| Alexander Fleming, Scotland | penicillin, the first antibiotic | discovered in 1928 |
| Rosalind Franklin, England | X-ray pictures of DNA | 1952 |
| Tim Berners-Lee, England | the World Wide Web | proposed in 1989 |

Fleming noticed in 1928 that a mould in one of his dishes had killed the bacteria around it. This accident was studied further by other scientists, and penicillin was developed into a medicine that has saved millions of lives. Many of these people worked to understand how the world works, so that others could use the knowledge.

sections.title: Grammar notes
paragraphs: **1. Active or passive.** Choose the active when the person matters: **Fleming discovered penicillin.** Choose the passive when the thing matters more: **Penicillin was discovered in 1928.** Add by to name the person: **The telephone was patented by Bell.** See Introduction to Grammar: Voice, reflexive and impersonal verbs.

**2. Purpose and result.** Say why someone did something with to and the base form of the verb, or with in order to for a more formal sound. Use so that when the purpose is a new clause. **Scientists did experiments to understand the world. They shared their results so that others could use them.** See Introduction to Grammar: Conjunctions and linking clauses.
**3. Word endings name people and things.** Many nouns are made from verbs, and the ending shows what kind of noun it is. See Introduction to Grammar: Word formation and register.

| Verb or noun | Person or thing | Ending |
| --- | --- | --- |
| invent | **inventor**, **invention** | -or and -ion |
| science | **scientist** | -ist |
| discover | **discoverer**, **discovery** | -er and -y |
| research | **researcher** | -er |

sections.title: Notice
paragraphs:
- A **discovery** is something that was already there and is found for the first time. An **invention** is something new that people make.
- Science is the subject and **a scientist** is the person. Do not say a science for a person.
- Dates for centuries use the: **in the nineteenth century**.

sections.title: Culture note
paragraphs: The Royal Society, founded in London in 1660, is one of the oldest scientific societies in the world. Many of the people in this lesson worked at universities or in societies like it, and many of them worked together or corresponded with one another across countries.
